ai-book-chat.title: AI Book Chat
ai-book-chat.summary: Upload a PDF and ask questions about it. Answers stream in with the pages they came from, backed by a local RAG pipeline.

problem.heading: Can you trust an answer about a long book?
problem.body: A plain chat model answers from general knowledge and cannot show where a claim comes from. For a long PDF you want answers grounded in the text, pages to check them against, and an honest signal when the book does not cover the question.

solution.heading: Retrieval with re-ranking and citations
solution.body: A worker parses the PDF, detects sections (outline first, then heading heuristics, then flat pages) and cuts chunks of about 600 tokens with 15% overlap that never cross a section boundary. Each question is rewritten into a standalone query from the recent turns, matched by cosine search in pgvector and re-ranked by an LLM before generation. Sources are streamed first, so the UI shows citations while the answer is still being written; when nothing relevant is found, the answer says so up front.

architecture.body: A React frontend talks HTTP and SSE to a FastAPI API backed by PostgreSQL with pgvector (HNSW, cosine). Uploads are queued in Redis and processed by a Celery worker: PyMuPDF parsing, chunking and batch embedding with local Ollama (nomic-embed-text). Chat, query rewriting and re-ranking use any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Groq by default. pnpm workspaces and Turborepo drive both apps.

lessons: Embeddings are deliberately not switchable: the vector column has a fixed width, so another model means a migration and a re-ingest. The app refuses to start when the configured dimensions and the column disagree, instead of returning plausible but meaningless results.

Follow-up questions like "and what about his brother?" only work because of the rewrite step; retrieval alone sees no context. Still out of scope: cross-document queries, OCR for scanned PDFs and accounts.

blind-clue.title: BlindClue
blind-clue.summary: Real-time multiplayer social deduction game: everyone gets the secret word except one player, who only gets a hint and has to blend in.
blind-clue.role: full stack: realtime backend, Vue frontend
blind-clue.effect: full game loop from lobby to scoring over WebSockets

problem.heading: A party game needs everyone in the same moment
problem.body: The game only works if all players move through the same phases together: describe the word, vote, reveal. Each phase has to reach every player as it happens, and the scoring has to be decided in one place.

solution.heading: A server-authoritative game over Socket.io
solution.body: Two to four players join a lobby and play three rounds of describing the word without naming it, then vote on who the impostor is. Votes are revealed, and a caught impostor can still score by guessing the word. The server owns the game state and the scoring; clients send events such as joinGame, submitDescription and voteImpostor and react to GameStarted, VotingStarted, VotesRevealed and GameEnded.

architecture.body: A pnpm monorepo: a Fastify + Socket.io + SQLite backend built in Clean Architecture layers (domain entities, use cases, application services, adapters) and a Vue 3 + Vite + Pinia + Tailwind frontend. Running games live in memory in a GameManager and are removed when they end; categories and words are managed through admin endpoints. The backend ships as a Docker image.

lessons: Keeping running games only in memory keeps the model simple; the flip side is that a restart would end the games in progress.
Returning a Result from every operation makes failure paths explicit and easy to test, including the scoring cases for a caught and an uncaught impostor.

perplex-image.title: PerplexImage
perplex-image.summary: Image puzzle game: pick a photo, rearrange the tiles with drag and drop and beat your own time and move count.
perplex-image.role: sole author: gameplay, state, API proxy, tests
perplex-image.effect: three difficulty levels, covered by unit and e2e tests

problem.heading: A puzzle that works on every screen
problem.body: Drag-and-drop puzzles are easy to build for a mouse and awkward everywhere else. The goal was a game that plays the same on mobile, tablet and desktop and never runs out of images to solve.

solution.heading: Tile puzzles on three difficulty levels
solution.body: Players choose an image from the Pexels API, pick a level (9×13, 15×23 or 20×30 tiles) and drag pieces into place while a timer and a move counter run. The game can be paused and reset, and it shows progress. Pinia holds the game state; a Nitro server route proxies Pexels so the API key stays on the server, and an adapter for Supabase storage exists next to the Pexels one.

architecture.body: Nuxt 3 with the Vue 3 Composition API, split into modules: core (shared utilities, store, types), game (pages, components, logic) and ui (generic components). Server routes under /server/api fetch images behind an adapter interface. Vitest covers units, Playwright covers end-to-end flows and Husky pre-commit hooks run the linter.

lessons: Keeping game logic in its own module, apart from generic UI components, keeps it testable with plain unit tests.
The image source sits behind an adapter, so Pexels and Supabase storage are interchangeable for the game.

ai-semantic-db.title: Semantic DB
ai-semantic-db.summary: CLI for local semantic search over your own structured data: define a schema, add records and search in plain language. No cloud, no API keys.
ai-semantic-db.role: design and implementation: schema model, CLI, embeddings, tests
ai-semantic-db.effect: records are searchable the moment they are saved

problem.heading: Semantic search without a cloud service
problem.body: Existing semantic search tools are cloud-based or tied to one data source. The aim was to define your own structure, keep the data on your machine and search it by meaning instead of by keyword.

solution.heading: Schema-driven collections with local embeddings
solution.body: A collection is defined with a compact field grammar such as price:float:embed:unit=PLN, supporting text, enum, int, float, bool, date and string array types. Each record is rendered into one formatted text card and embedded with bge-m3 through Ollama on save, so added means searchable. Search is cosine top-k with a Rich table and an --explain mode; it refuses to run when a collection was embedded with a different model, because cross-model distances mean nothing.

architecture.body: A Python 3.12 CLI built with Typer on a layered structure: domain, application (ports and use cases), infrastructure (SQLAlchemy, Alembic, Ollama client) and cli, with import-linter contracts keeping dependencies pointing inward. Records are JSONB payloads in PostgreSQL 17 with pgvector (halfvec 1024), so schemas change without per-collection DDL. Writes are use cases; reads go through a single queries facade.

lessons: JSONB payloads instead of per-collection tables trade some speed for far simpler migrations and arbitrary schemas.
Storing the exact rendered text next to each vector prevents silent drift when a template changes after embeddings exist.

quiz-forge.title: Quiz Forge
quiz-forge.summary: Full-stack quiz app: users browse and play quizzes, admins manage content in a dashboard. A TypeScript monorepo with Nuxt 4 and NestJS.
quiz-forge.role: full stack: NestJS API, Nuxt frontend, auth, tests
quiz-forge.effect: JWT auth with role-based access and a documented REST API

problem.heading: Quizzes need a player side and an admin side
problem.body: A quiz app has two audiences: players who browse, play and submit answers, and admins who create the question sets. Each needs its own access rules and its own screens.

solution.heading: A role-based quiz platform
solution.body: Users sign in with JWT access and refresh tokens kept in HTTP-only cookies. Admins create quizzes with questions and answer options; players pick a quiz, play it and submit their responses. Server-side guards enforce the admin and user roles, quiz listings are paginated and Swagger documents the API. The interface has a Polish locale.

architecture.body: A Turborepo + pnpm monorepo. apps/backend is a NestJS REST API on TypeORM and PostgreSQL 15 with auth, quiz and user modules; apps/frontend is a layer-based Nuxt 4 app (core, base, auth) with Tailwind and Pinia. Shared DTOs live in a shared-types package. Vitest covers units, Playwright covers end-to-end flows and Docker Compose runs the database.

lessons: Shared TypeScript DTOs in one package keep the frontend and backend contracts in sync.
Splitting the Nuxt app into core, base and auth layers keeps layouts and i18n apart from the feature pages.

lean-track.title: LeanTrack
lean-track.summary: Calorie and macro tracker: set goals, log meals in a daily diary and monitor progress. Vue 3 frontend, Fastify API, PostgreSQL.
lean-track.role: full stack: Fastify API, Vue frontend, database
lean-track.effect: diary, products and goals behind an authenticated API

problem.heading: Tracking nutrition without friction
problem.body: Staying on track means seeing calories and macros against your goals every day, with as little effort as possible when logging a meal.

solution.heading: Goals, products and a daily diary
solution.body: Users register and sign in, set nutrition goals, manage a list of products and add food diary entries. The API exposes auth, products, diary and goals endpoints, and the frontend is organised by the same features.

architecture.body: A pnpm monorepo with a Fastify + TypeORM backend (feature modules for auth, diary, products and goals; config for environment, JWT and database; migrations) and a Vue 3 + Vite frontend split into features, shared code and the router. PostgreSQL runs in Docker Compose. Both apps use TypeScript strict mode, ESLint, Prettier and Vitest.

lessons: Mirroring the backend modules in frontend features keeps each feature easy to find on both sides.
A PRD, a tech spec and user-flow diagrams sit in docs/ next to the code, so the intent behind each module stays on record.

match-colours.title: Match Colours
match-colours.summary: Colour memory game: click the colours in the order they appeared to reach the next level. Difficulty grows and scores are tracked.
match-colours.effect: playable in the browser on any screen size

problem.heading: A small game to practise a real app structure
problem.body: Match Colours was built for fun and learning: a simple idea with enough state (sequences, levels, scores) to practise structuring a Nuxt application.

solution.heading: Remember the sequence, repeat it in order
solution.body: Players are shown a sequence of colours and click them back in the same order to advance. Later levels bring more challenging sequences, scores are tracked between attempts and the layout is responsive.

architecture.body: A Nuxt 3 and Vue 3 application made of pages, components, composables, stores and server routes, deployed on Vercel.

lessons: Putting state in stores and reusable logic in composables keeps the pages thin.
A game this small still benefits from tests; later projects such as PerplexImage add Vitest and Playwright coverage.

sudoku.title: Sudoku
sudoku.summary: Browser Sudoku with several difficulty levels, instant move validation and a timer. Built with Next.js.
sudoku.effect: playable online with validation and a timer

problem.heading: Sudoku that checks you as you play
problem.body: Pen-and-paper Sudoku gives no feedback until you finish. A web version can validate every move and time the run.

solution.heading: An interactive board with instant feedback
solution.body: Players enter numbers and move between cells on a dynamic board, choose a difficulty from easy to hard and get immediate feedback from built-in validation. An integrated timer tracks the solving time.

architecture.body: A Next.js 14 and React 18 application in TypeScript, structured as pages, components, hooks, reducers and context, with a Prisma schema and seed data. Docker files are included and a static export is published on GitHub Pages.

lessons: Reducers and context keep the board state in one place, away from the cell components.
A static export on GitHub Pages is enough hosting for a client-side game.

screencaster.title: Screencaster
screencaster.summary: Write a YAML script, run one command, get a narrated MP4 of a website. Renders run in Docker with Playwright, offline Piper voices and ffmpeg; an MCP server lets Claude Code create demos from chat.
screencaster.role: design and implementation: Go CLI, MCP server, render pipeline
screencaster.effect: narrated demo videos from a YAML script, rendered without an LLM

problem.heading: Demo videos never get made
problem.body: Recording, voiceover and editing by hand cost too much, so release notes ship without video. Every UI change would mean recording again.

solution.heading: A demo is a script, not a recording
solution.body: A demo is described in plain language, Claude Code writes it as a YAML script, and the CLI or MCP server renders it. Playwright performs the steps in a browser, a local Piper voice narrates each step as its action starts and ffmpeg assembles the MP4. Rendering makes no LLM call, so the same script replays the same demo, and a UI change means fixing one step and rendering again.

architecture.body: A single Go module with a layered internal/ tree: pure domain rules, use cases behind ports, and one adapter per external tool (Playwright, Piper, ffmpeg, SQLite, MCP). The screencaster CLI and the MCP server share one render pipeline, and everything runs in one Docker image.

lessons: Keeping rendering free of LLM calls makes a demo a replayable artifact: same script, same steps, same timing.
One process and one SQLite file are enough for a tool a single developer runs, so the design skips scaling concerns.
